unit.title: The 2026 reset
unit.summary: The new cars: active aero, the 50/50 power unit, Overtake Mode and the new teams.

lessons.title: Why F1 reset the rules
lessons.objective: Explain what a regulation era is and what 2026 was meant to change.

payload.prompt: What is a regulation era in F1?

options.text: A multi-year rulebook cycle; a new one means big redesigns and a reshuffled pecking order.
options.explanation: Right. A new era means new rules for everyone, so teams redesign their cars and the order can shake up.

options.text: A single season where the rules change slightly.
options.explanation: No, regulation eras last multiple years. Rule tweaks happen within an era.

options.text: A penalty for breaking the FIA regulations.
options.explanation: That is a grid penalty or points deduction, not a regulation era.

options.text: A requirement to change engines every other year.
options.explanation: Engine supply is set within an era, but a regulation era is about the whole rulebook.

explanation.correct: Right. A regulation era lasts several years with a broadly fixed rulebook. When a new one starts, the cars and power units are redesigned and the pecking order can reshuffle.
explanation.incorrect: A regulation era is a multi-year rulebook cycle. 2026 begins a new one, so car design and performance hierarchies reset.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 begins a new regulation era.

payload.prompt: Why did F1 reset the rules for 2026?

options.text: To make the cars greener, smaller and more equal in power, and to welcome new engine suppliers and teams.
options.explanation: Right. 2026 was designed to reset the grid and bring in new manufacturers and sustainable technology.

options.text: Because Mercedes and Red Bull were too fast.
options.explanation: Regulation changes do reset the order, but the stated goal was sustainability and new entrants.

options.text: To make the races shorter.
options.explanation: Race distance is unchanged. The reset is about car design and power units.

options.text: To reduce the cost cap.
options.explanation: The cost cap stays roughly the same. 2026 is about new rules, not cheaper racing.

explanation.correct: Right. 2026 brought active aero, a 50/50 power split, sustainable fuel, smaller lighter cars, and new teams like Audi and Cadillac.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 reset welcomed new engine makers (Audi, Honda, Red Bull-Ford) and was built around sustainability and a 50/50 power unit.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 reset to bring in new manufacturers and greener technology.

payload.prompt: Match each 2026 goal to what it means.

pairs.definition: A multi-year rulebook cycle; 2026 begins a new one with fresh car designs and reset power hierarchies.
A yearly limit on team spending (roughly $215 million) to keep budgets fair and racing competitive.
100% advanced fuel made from non-food biomass, waste or captured carbon, not fossil fuels.

distractorDefinitions: A penalty for breaking F1's environmental rules.
A system that recycles old tyres into fuel.

explanation.summary: The 2026 reset is about a new rulebook, fairer budgets and greener fuel. All three work together.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 is greener, fairer and reset.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: Why do they always change the rules?

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: A regulation era lasts several years; when it ends, the rulebook resets and the grid shakes up.
options.explanation: Exactly. A regulation era is the why.

options.text: The rules change every few years to keep things fresh.
options.explanation: It is more than that. A regulation era is a planned multi-year reset.

options.text: They change the rules because it is boring otherwise.
options.explanation: That is not the reason. Regulation eras are strategic resets, not whim.

payload.translation: A regulation era is a multi-year rulebook cycle that resets the grid and opens doors to new teams and technologies.

followUps.line: So the grid gets shaken up when a new era starts?
followUps.why: Yes, and it is on purpose. The old dominant team may lose an edge.

followUps.line: Did 2026 reset because the old cars were unfair?
followUps.why: Not unfair, but the ground-effect cars were too complex. 2026 reset to bring new manufacturers and greener tech.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A regulation era is not gossip; it is F1 strategy. Ask why they changed specific things, not guesses.

lessons.title: Smaller, lighter, narrower cars
lessons.objective: Describe how the 2026 cars differ in size, weight and downforce.

payload.prompt: Guess: what is the minimum weight of a 2026 F1 car and driver, in kilograms?

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026 cars are lighter at 768 kg minimum, down about 30 kg from the 2022 to 2025 era. Smaller, narrower and lighter.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 minimum weight is 768 kilograms, about 30 kilograms lighter than the previous era. That is a deliberate reset.
explanation.sayThisLine: The minimum weight dropped for 2026.

payload.prompt: Why are the 2026 cars smaller and lighter?

options.text: To reduce downforce and drag for efficiency and to level out the grid after years of dominance by heavy, downforce-heavy cars.
options.explanation: Right. The massive ground-effect cars of 2022-2025 were too dominant; 2026 goes lighter and less reliant on ground effect.

options.text: To make the cars faster and more spectacular.
options.explanation: The goal is balance and efficiency, not raw speed. Lighter and smaller means less downforce, not more.

options.text: Because narrower tyres are cheaper.
options.explanation: Tyre cost is handled by Pirelli separately. Smaller cars are a design philosophy for 2026.

options.text: To make it easier for new teams to enter.
options.explanation: Smaller is simpler, but the main goal was to reset performance after years of ground-effect dominance.

explanation.correct: Right. The 2022–2025 cars were massive, heavy and all about ground effect. 2026 resets by going smaller, lighter and less dependent on one technology.
explanation.incorrect: The 2022-2025 cars became increasingly ground-effect-dependent. 2026 scales back: smaller, lighter, less downforce, more balance.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 cars are smaller and lighter by design.

payload.prompt: What is ground effect, and how does it change for 2026?

options.text: Air under the floor is shaped to create suction, pushing the car down. 2026 cars use it less, relying more on active aero.
options.explanation: Right. The 2022-2025 cars were ground-effect machines; 2026 dials it back and uses wings that move instead.

options.text: Ground effect is when the track is bumpy and affects handling. 2026 tracks are smoother.
options.explanation: No, ground effect is aerodynamic. It is the shaped floor that creates downforce by speeding air underneath.

options.text: It is the effect of low fuel loads on lap time. 2026 allows more fuel.
options.explanation: That is not ground effect. Ground effect is how the underfloor creates downforce.

options.text: It is a safety system that stops the car if it gets too low. 2026 removed it.
options.explanation: That is not ground effect. The shaped floor creating suction is ground effect.

explanation.correct: Right. Ground effect is the shaped floor that speeds air underneath, creating a vacuum that sucks the car down. 2026 uses less of it.
explanation.incorrect: Ground effect is aerodynamic suction from the underfloor. The 2022-2025 cars were ground-effect dominated; 2026 relies more on active wings.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ground effect pulls the car down; 2026 uses active aero instead.

payload.prompt: Do the 2026 cars have less downforce than the 2022-2025 cars?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car with active aero wings.

explanation.correct: Right. 2026 cars have less total downforce than 2022-2025. The reset was to reduce reliance on ground effect and massive wings.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. 2026 cars are deliberately lighter and have less downforce, which is why they are less dependent on ground effect and need active aero to manage it.

payload.prompt: Are the 2026 car floors narrower than they were in 2022-2025?

scene.alt: A top-down view of a 2026 F1 car showing the width of the floor.

explanation.correct: Right. The floor is narrower in 2026, which reduces ground-effect suction and forces the cars to rely more on wing adjustments.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the 2026 floor is narrower, which reduces ground effect and is one of the ways the cars are made smaller overall.

lessons.title: The 50/50 power unit
lessons.objective: Explain what the power unit is made of now and what disappeared.

payload.prompt: Match each part of the 2026 power unit to what it does.

pairs.definition: The 1.6-litre turbocharged V6 petrol engine, producing roughly 400 kW in 2026.
Recovers braking energy and adds up to 350 kW from the battery, with strict per-lap limits.
The high-voltage battery holding harvested energy for deployment during a lap.

distractorDefinitions: A heat-recovery system on the turbo charger.
A fuel tank that stores sustainable fuel.

explanation.summary: The 2026 power unit is roughly 50/50: combustion engine and MGU-K electrical system sharing the work.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is the engine plus the battery, about half and half.

payload.prompt: What did the MGU-H do, and why is it gone in 2026?

pairs.definition: The motor-generator unit on the turbo's heat exchanger that recovered waste heat from the exhaust. Removed for 2026.
Simplifying the power unit and bringing back a touch of turbo lag to increase driver skill and racing.
The MGU-K motor-generator (on the drivetrain) now does all the electrical recovery, with more power to compensate.

distractorDefinitions: The MGU-H was unreliable and teams wanted it gone.
It was removed to reduce fuel consumption.

explanation.summary: The MGU-H was complex and reliable; removing it simplifies the power unit and adds a tiny bit of turbo lag, which challenges drivers more.
explanation.sayThisLine: MGU-H is gone, so more turbo lag and simpler power units.

payload.prompt: Where is the MGU-K on a 2026 F1 car, relative to the engine?

diagram.alt: Side view of a Formula 1 car showing the cockpit, halo, engine and rear suspension.

explanation.correct: Right. The MGU-K is on the drivetrain, recovering energy from braking through the wheels.
explanation.incorrect: The MGU-K sits on the gearbox or drivetrain, where it can harvest braking energy from the wheels and add power to the drivetrain.

payload.prompt: Where would the energy store (battery) be mounted on a 2026 car?

diagram.alt: Top-down view of a Formula 1 car showing the chassis, cockpit and rear.

hotspots.label: Inside the monocoque near the driver
Near the gearbox at the rear

explanation.correct: Right. The battery is mounted inside the monocoque for safety and weight distribution, close to the driver.
explanation.incorrect: The energy store is housed in the monocoque for protection and to keep weight centralised. It is inside, not mounted externally.

payload.prompt: What does '50/50 power unit' mean in 2026?

options.text: The combustion engine and electrical system (MGU-K) each contribute roughly half the power, about 400 kW and 350 kW.
options.explanation: Right. The petrol engine does half, the battery-electrical system does half. It is a genuine balance.

options.text: Half the cars run on electricity and half on petrol.
options.explanation: No, every car is hybrid: petrol engine plus electrical system. It is not half and half by car count.

options.text: The engine and gearbox share equal power.
options.explanation: The gearbox transfers power; the 50/50 is about combustion versus electrical energy.

options.text: The 2026 cars are half as powerful as the 2025 cars.
options.explanation: No, the total power output is comparable. The split is how the power is generated: petrol and electric.

explanation.correct: Right. 2026 is designed so the combustion engine and the electrical system (battery and MGU-K) share the power output roughly equally.
explanation.incorrect: The 50/50 split means the petrol V6 and the electrical system (recovery and deployment) contribute similar power. It is a deliberate balance.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is roughly half from the engine, half from the battery.

lessons.title: Straight Mode and Corner Mode
lessons.objective: Explain how active aero works and how it differs from DRS.

payload.prompt: What is active aero?

options.text: Wings that move during a lap to switch between high downforce and low drag, giving the driver control over balance all lap long.
options.explanation: Right. Active aero lets drivers adjust the wings mid-lap, trading downforce for speed on straights, then opening it back up for corners.

options.text: A system that automatically optimises the wings for each corner.
options.explanation: Not automatic; the driver or team chooses when to switch modes based on the track layout.

options.text: Flexible wings that bend under load to reduce drag.
options.explanation: That is flexi-wings, a loophole. Active aero is deliberate adjustable wings.

options.text: The same as DRS, just renamed for 2026.
options.explanation: No. DRS was a one-use flap in certain zones; active aero is available all lap for constant strategy.

explanation.correct: Right. Active aero is new for 2026: wings that the driver or team can open and close to balance downforce and drag throughout the lap.
explanation.incorrect: Active aero means moveable wing elements that can be adjusted during a lap. Unlike DRS (which is gone), it is available everywhere and continuously.
explanation.sayThisLine: Active aero lets you open the wings for speed on straights.

payload.prompt: What is Straight Mode (also called X-mode)?

options.text: A low-drag wing setting where the front and rear wings open to reduce drag on straights, allowed in designated zones.
options.explanation: Right. Straight Mode is the flat-wing setup: less downforce, less drag, more top speed.

options.text: A system that works only on long straights, not short ones.
options.explanation: Straight Mode is allowed in circuit-specific zones, not just long straights.

options.text: A mode where the car drives in a straight line automatically.
options.explanation: No, Straight Mode is just the wing position. The driver still drives.

options.text: A penalty box where cars are sent for rule breaks.
options.explanation: That is not related to modes. Straight Mode is an aero setting.

explanation.correct: Right. Straight Mode means the wings open flat for minimal drag. It is called X-mode by fans and is used to gain top speed on designated straights.
explanation.incorrect: Straight Mode (X-mode) is the low-downforce, low-drag wing setting for straights. It opens the wings to reduce resistance.
explanation.sayThisLine: Straight mode on the back straight and boom, he is gone.

payload.prompt: Does Corner Mode (Z-mode) give more downforce than Straight Mode?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car with wings in high-downforce position before a corner.

explanation.correct: Right. Corner Mode (Z-mode) is high downforce: the wings close up to generate grip for braking and turning.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Corner Mode is the high-downforce setting, the opposite of Straight Mode, used for corners and braking zones.

payload.prompt: Can drivers use active aero on every part of the lap, or only in certain zones?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car with wings adjusting mid-lap.

explanation.correct: Right. Straight Mode is only allowed in FIA-approved zones on each circuit, not everywhere. You cannot use it mid-corner.
explanation.incorrect: Active aero is restricted to specific zones on each circuit. The FIA decides where Straight Mode is legal to keep racing fair and safe.

lessons.title: Overtake Mode and Boost
lessons.objective: Explain who gets Overtake Mode and how Boost differs.

payload.prompt: Who can use Overtake Mode in 2026?

options.text: A driver within one second of the car directly ahead at a detection point on the track.
options.explanation: Right. Overtake Mode is available to any driver who is within one second of the car ahead, not just at certain zones.

options.text: Only the car ahead, to defend.
options.explanation: No, it is for the follower. The car ahead cannot activate Overtake Mode.

options.text: Any driver at any time.
options.explanation: No, you must be within one second of the car ahead to qualify.

options.text: Only on long straights, like Monaco.
options.explanation: Overtake Mode is based on gap, not track layout. It works at any track.

explanation.correct: Right. Overtake Mode is automatic for any car within one second of the car ahead. It is DRS's replacement but fairer.
explanation.incorrect: Overtake Mode activates for any driver trailing by one second or less at the detection point. It replaced DRS for 2026.
explanation.sayThisLine: Within one second, you get Overtake Mode.

payload.prompt: What is the Boost button?

options.text: A manual driver button that allows extra electrical deployment for a burst of speed, limited in use per race.
options.explanation: Right. Boost is an extra tool: the driver hits it to deploy more battery power, but it is rationed so it cannot be used every lap.

options.text: An automatic system that gives more power if you are falling behind.
options.explanation: No, Boost is manual and limited. The driver chooses when to use it.

options.text: The same as Overtake Mode, just a different name.
options.explanation: Overtake Mode and Boost are different. Overtake Mode is automatic for trailing cars; Boost is manual.

options.text: A penalty that adds speed to a car that has broken a rule.
options.explanation: Boost is a tool, not a penalty. It gives the driver more control over energy deployment.

explanation.correct: Right. Boost is a driver-activated button to deploy extra battery power. It is limited per race, so teams and drivers must choose when to use it.
explanation.incorrect: Boost is a manual electrical deployment tool: the driver presses a button for extra speed, but it can only be used a limited number of times per race.
explanation.sayThisLine: He hit the boost button on the last lap.

payload.prompt: Is Overtake Mode only available in certain FIA-approved zones, like Straight Mode?

scene.alt: A car within one second of the car ahead, ready to use Overtake Mode.

explanation.correct: Right. Overtake Mode is available anywhere on the track if you are within one second. There are no zone restrictions.
explanation.incorrect: Overtake Mode works everywhere, unlike Straight Mode which is zone-restricted. If you are within one second, you get it automatically anywhere.

payload.prompt: Can a driver use the Boost button as many times as they want during a race?

scene.alt: A driver reaching for the boost button on the steering wheel.

explanation.correct: Right. Boost is limited: a team gets a certain number of deploys per race, so they must use it wisely.
explanation.incorrect: No, Boost is rationed. Teams get a limited allocation per race, so strategy and timing matter a lot.

payload.prompt: Use Boost now to pass, or save it for the final stint?

situation.narrative: You are chasing the car ahead, 0.9 seconds behind, on lap 35 of 71. Overtake Mode is active. The next straight is a good passing spot, but you have only two Boost uses left for the entire race.

options.label: Deploy Boost to pass now
options.consequence: You pass, gaining track position, but have only one Boost use left. If he fights back later, you have limited firepower.
considerations: Costs a Boost use mid-race when the field is still competitive
You have half the race left where Boost might be more critical

options.label: Rely on Overtake Mode, save Boost
options.consequence: You stay in second with Overtake Mode alone, but preserve your Boost ammunition for the closing laps when gaps tighten and passes matter most.
considerations: Overtake Mode alone may not be enough, so you may not pass today
Keeps both Boosts for critical moments in the final stint
Strategy depends on reliability: if he pits or slows, you may benefit anyway

payload.expertNote: Boost timing is strategy like pit windows. Using Boost to pass mid-race feels good but can leave you vulnerable late. The best drivers save it for when the race is won or lost, not just because it is available.
payload.sayThisLine: Save the Boost for when you really need it.

lessons.title: Recharging: where the energy comes from
lessons.objective: Say where a car harvests energy and what it costs.

payload.prompt: Where does a 2026 car harvest energy during a lap?

options.text: Mainly under braking, using the MGU-K on the drivetrain, and from engine power when cruising.
options.explanation: Right. Braking is the big source: wheels slow down, the MGU-K captures that kinetic energy. The engine also feeds power in steady phases.

options.text: Only on straights by coasting.
options.explanation: Coasting helps, but braking is the main harvest point. Corners do not harvest much energy.

options.text: From the turbo's waste heat, like the MGU-H did.
options.explanation: The MGU-H is gone in 2026. Harvesting is through the drivetrain (MGU-K) now.

options.text: Automatically without any cost to the driver.
options.explanation: Braking recovers energy, but aggressive harvesting through lift-and-coast costs lap time.

explanation.correct: Right. Braking under the MGU-K is the main harvest. The driver can also lift off and coast to recharge the battery, which costs speed.
explanation.incorrect: The MGU-K on the drivetrain harvests braking energy. Additionally, drivers can lift and coast to top up the battery, trading speed for energy.
explanation.sayThisLine: Braking is where you harvest energy.

payload.prompt: Match each energy strategy to what it means.

pairs.definition: Refilling the battery from braking and engine power, done constantly during every lap.
When the battery runs out on a straight, the car stops getting electrical help and even slows as it forces a recharge.
Easing off the throttle early before braking to let the battery recharge and save fuel.

distractorDefinitions: Coasting down from a mountain without power.

explanation.summary: Energy management is the race: teams harvest on brakes, deploy on straights, and lift to recharge. Clipping is the price of an empty battery.
explanation.sayThisLine: Recharge under braking, deploy on the straight, clip if you run out.

payload.prompt: What does lift-and-coast cost a driver?

options.text: Lap time: easing off throttle early loses speed, but saves energy for later deployment.
options.explanation: Right. Lift-and-coast is a trade: give up a tenth now to bank energy for deployment later.

options.text: Nothing; it is a free way to recharge.
options.explanation: It is not free. Lifting off throttle early, before you would normally brake, costs lap time.

options.text: Engine power; the car downshifts and loses rpm.
options.explanation: Lift-and-coast is about throttle management, not downshifting. The cost is lap time from a slower exit.

options.text: Tyre temperature; cooling the tyres hurts grip.
options.explanation: Tyres may cool slightly, but the main cost of lift-and-coast is the lap time lost.

explanation.correct: Right. Lift-and-coast sacrifices a tenth or two of lap time to top up the battery for later. Teams calculate if it is worth it.
explanation.incorrect: Lift-and-coast costs lap time by forcing an earlier-than-usual ease off. The driver banks that energy for use on the next straight.

payload.prompt: What happens if a 2026 car's battery is already full and cannot harvest more energy?

options.text: Energy harvested under braking is wasted; the car cannot store it, so it just slows naturally.
options.explanation: Right. A full battery cannot accept a charge. Braking will slow the car (as normal) but the MGU-K cannot capture that energy.

options.text: The car automatically starts depleting energy to make room.
options.explanation: No, the battery does not auto-deploy to make room. Wasted braking energy is simply lost.

options.text: The team can press a button to dump excess energy as heat.
options.explanation: There is no dump button. If the battery is full, harvest attempts just fail and energy is wasted.

options.text: The car gains extra grip from the full battery.
options.explanation: No, a full battery does not give extra grip. The energy cannot be used until it is deployed.

explanation.correct: Right. A full battery cannot absorb any more charge. Braking still slows the car, but the MGU-K cannot harvest that kinetic energy.
explanation.incorrect: If the battery is full, harvesting is blocked. Energy from braking is wasted as heat instead of being stored.

lessons.title: Sustainable fuel
lessons.objective: Explain what sustainable fuel is and what it changes for fans.

payload.prompt: What is sustainable fuel in 2026 F1?

options.text: 100% advanced fuel made from non-food biomass, waste or captured carbon, not fossil fuel.
options.explanation: Right. It is a real zero-carbon or carbon-neutral fuel, not just a greenwash label.

options.text: Electric fuel that does not burn.
options.explanation: F1 2026 still uses a combustion engine; the fuel itself is different, but it still burns.

options.text: Fuel mixed with 50% electricity.
options.explanation: No, sustainable fuel is a type of petrol. The electricity comes from the MGU-K battery separately.

options.text: Cheaper fuel to reduce team costs.
options.explanation: Sustainable fuel may cost more initially. It is about environmental impact, not budget.

explanation.correct: Right. Sustainable fuel for 2026 is a real zero-carbon drop-in replacement for fossil fuel, made from sustainable sources.
explanation.incorrect: Sustainable fuel is produced from advanced biomass, agricultural waste, or captured carbon, and burns in standard engines. It is 100% sustainable by 2026.
explanation.sayThisLine: The fuel is 100% sustainable now, not fossil fuel.

payload.prompt: Why did F1 switch to 100% sustainable fuel for 2026?

options.text: To reduce carbon emissions and show that performance racing can be sustainable, and to push fuel manufacturers to innovate.
options.explanation: Right. F1 is a leader in technology; showing sustainable fuel can power high performance is a big statement.

options.text: Because fossil fuels will run out soon.
options.explanation: That is part of it, but the main reason is climate leadership and pushing the industry.

options.text: To make the engines less powerful.
options.explanation: Sustainable fuel does not reduce power; the engines stay the same.

options.text: To save money on fuel.
options.explanation: Sustainable fuel may cost more. It is about environmental impact and leadership.

explanation.correct: Right. F1 switched to 100% sustainable fuel to demonstrate that high-performance racing can be carbon-neutral and to push fuel technology forward.
explanation.incorrect: F1 switched to 100% sustainable fuel for 2026 to reduce carbon emissions and to show that performance and sustainability are compatible.
explanation.sayThisLine: Sustainable fuel is a climate leadership move.

payload.prompt: Fill in: 2026 F1 fuel is {{fuel-type}}, made from biomass, waste or captured carbon.
payload.template: Fill in: 2026 F1 fuel is {{fuel-type}}, made from biomass, waste or captured carbon.

explanation.correct: Right. Sustainable fuel is the correct term for 2026 F1's eco-friendly fuel option.
explanation.incorrect: The term is sustainable fuel. It is a real drop-in replacement for fossil fuel, not synthetic or electric.

payload.prompt: For fans, 2026 sustainable fuel means {{thing}} with {{impact}} carbon impact.
payload.template: For fans, 2026 sustainable fuel means {{thing}} with {{impact}} carbon impact.

explanation.correct: Right. The car experience is unchanged for fans (still a V6 roar), but the carbon footprint is much lower.
explanation.incorrect: Sustainable fuel does not change how the car feels or sounds; it just lowers the carbon emissions. The V6 engine is the same.

lessons.title: Audi, Cadillac, Ford, Honda: who is new
lessons.objective: Identify the new teams and engine partnerships.

payload.prompt: Match each new entrant to their role in 2026.

pairs.definition: A new works team building its own car and power unit; will compete as Audi in the constructors' championship.
The 11th team for 2026, starting on Ferrari engines and later moving to General Motors power.
A new engine supplier partnering with Red Bull and Racing Bulls teams for 2026 onwards.

distractorDefinitions: An engine that runs on liquid hydrogen.
A team that makes parts for other constructors.

explanation.summary: Audi is a works team, Cadillac is an 11th-team entry, and Ford is a power unit partner. The 2026 grid expanded.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 brought new teams and new engine makers.

payload.prompt: Match each engine supplier to the teams using it.

pairs.definition: Supplies engines to Haas and Cadillac (starting), plus its own Ferrari works team.
Supplies engines to McLaren, Williams and Alpine, plus its own Mercedes works team.
A new engine partner for Aston Martin in a works-style relationship for 2026.

distractorDefinitions: Supplies engines to exactly one team per manufacturer.
Does not sell engines to customer teams.

explanation.summary: Engine suppliers in 2026 are Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda (new), Audi, and Red Bull-Ford. Most supply multiple teams.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi and Red Bull-Ford power the 2026 grid.

payload.prompt: What makes Audi special as a new team in 2026?

options.text: Audi is a works team building its own engine and car, not a customer team buying power from elsewhere.
options.explanation: Right. Audi is a manufacturer entering with full works team status: it owns the power unit technology.

options.text: Audi buys engines from Ferrari.
options.explanation: No, Audi makes its own power unit. That is what makes it a works team.

options.text: Audi is replacing an existing team.
options.explanation: Audi took over Sauber, but entered F1 as a works manufacturer, not just a rebrand.

options.text: Audi is only on the grid for one season.
options.explanation: No, Audi is a long-term commitment as a power unit maker and works team.

explanation.correct: Right. Audi is a works team with its own power unit factory and development. That is rare and prestigious.
explanation.incorrect: Audi is a works team and engine manufacturer for 2026, not a customer team. It builds and owns its own power unit technology.
explanation.sayThisLine: Audi is a new works team and power unit maker.

payload.prompt: Why is Cadillac an 11th team for 2026 instead of 10?

options.text: The FIA approved an 11th team entry to bring racing to North America and open the grid to new manufacturers.
options.explanation: Right. Cadillac and General Motors' entry signals F1's North American expansion and new competition.

options.text: Because one of the existing teams left F1.
options.explanation: No, all other teams stayed. Cadillac is an addition, not a replacement.

options.text: To match the number of constructors to the number of engine makers.
options.explanation: That is not why. Cadillac's entry was independent of the engine supplier count.

options.text: Cadillac is just a temporary partner team.
options.explanation: Cadillac is a permanent entry with Perez and Bottas as drivers, not a temporary guest.

explanation.correct: Right. Cadillac and GM's entry for 2026 marks the first new team in several years and reflects F1's push into the North American market.
explanation.incorrect: Cadillac was approved as the 11th team for 2026 to expand racing into North America and compete for both drivers' and constructors' championships.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cadillac is the 11th team, a new North American entry.

payload.prompt: Which of these are new engine suppliers entering F1 for 2026?

diagram.alt: Logos representing F1 engine makers and manufacturers.

explanation.correct: Right. Audi, Honda and Red Bull-Ford are new. Mercedes, Ferrari and Alpine continue from before.
explanation.incorrect: Audi (works team), Honda (Aston Martin) and Red Bull-Ford are new. Mercedes and Ferrari already supplied engines; Alpine switched from Renault power to Mercedes.

payload.prompt: In 2026, F1 has {{num}} engine suppliers: Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi and {{new-one}}.
payload.template: In 2026, F1 has {{num}} engine suppliers: Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi and {{new-one}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Five engine suppliers in 2026: the big three (Ferrari, Mercedes) plus three new makers (Honda, Audi, Red Bull-Ford).
explanation.incorrect: Five suppliers for 2026: Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi and Red Bull-Ford. Alpine switched to Mercedes power for 2026.
